Example [09](09-rank1-modal-mimo.qmd) demonstrates the joint-MIMO modal fit on a teaching
plant. This page runs the same step on the real thing: the SRM is an HSTS suspension, and
it is identified here through its real production L1-SRM top-mass dampers — the foton
`SRM_M1_DAMP_<dof>` banks (from `L1SUSSRM.txt`, engaged FMs from the archived L1 SDF) — closed
around the shared bare-M1 6×6 HSTS plant on the compiled [`rtsfreerun`](https://controlsystems.docs.ligo.org/rtsfreerun)
twin. No hardware; no method change. One Pintelon–Schoukens multisine is driven through each
closed loop, the open-loop coupled plant is recovered through the loops, and the package's
rank-1 modal fit returns the shared modal table.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What makes this page different from 09
The plant is the compiled `x1hsts6dof` CDS composite, not a Python lumped model, and the loops
are the real L1-SRM damping banks — not idealized velocity dampers. Because the compiled
model is not installed in CI, this page is `freeze: true`: the slow MIMO campaign (one multisine
per DoF through the closed loops, ~13 min on the twin) runs once and is cached locally; the
figures below re-run only the fast offline fit against that cache and are scored against an
analytic state-space oracle derived from the twin's own filter definitions.
:::

## The measurement design — resolution is set by the ringdown

The method point of this page comes before any fitting: the campaign's frequency
resolution was not guessed, it was derived from the prior. A mode `(f₀, Q)` has FWHM
`Δf = f₀/Q` and a ringdown time constant `τ = Q/(π f₀)`. To resolve `Q` — not just `f₀` — the
parametric fit needs several frequency bins across each resonance, i.e.
`df ≤ Δf / (a few bins)`. Since `df = 1/T`, that demands a period `T ≳ (bins)·Q/f₀`. This is
just the Pintelon–Schoukens rule that the segment length must exceed the plant time constant
for a leakage-free FRF, read through the prior's slowest-ringing mode.

`system_ident.design.resolution.recommend_resolution` formalizes this. Calling it on the prior
HSTS modes (the resolvable design set, Q≈50 — the real SRM's Qs are much larger, and this
uniform low Q is carried for ease of calculation) turns the physics into the concrete
campaign knobs:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "What resolution does the prior demand to resolve Q?"
display(Markdown(
    f"For these HSTS modes (`Q≈50`), `recommend_resolution` returns "
    f"**df = {h.reco_df:.4f} Hz** — a **{h.reco_period:.0f} s** period. The campaign run here "
    f"used **df = {h.used_df:.4f} Hz** ({h.used_period:.0f} s/period), the **finest feasible** "
    f"grid (~13 min total twin time across the six DoFs). Frequencies recover in a short record; "
    f"**Q is gated by the ringdown** — high-Q suspension modes ring for a long time, so resolving "
    f"Q is a long record. The narrowest peak (the 0.67 Hz / Q≈50 mode) has FWHM ≈ 13 mHz, so "
    f"several bins across it — the fine 0.004 Hz grid — are needed to pin its Q."))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-srm-resolution
#| fig-cap: "Mode separation Δf and ringdown time τ for each prior mode, with the achieved and recommended frequency resolution df. The record length is set from τ rather than guessed."
#| code-summary: "Δf and ringdown τ per prior mode, with the achieved and recommended df"
srm.resolution_design_fig()
```

Each blue marker is a prior mode's FWHM; the gold line is the achieved `df`, the rose dotted line
is what `recommend_resolution` asks for. The green diamonds are the ringdowns — the lowest modes
ring for hundreds of seconds, which is exactly why a fine `df` (a long period) is unavoidable to
pin their `Q`.

## Open-loop recovery through the real damping loops

The campaign drives each `DRIVE_EXC_<dof>` with a P&S multisine and reads all six reconstructed
plant inputs (`X = drive − damper feedback`) and all six readouts (`Y`) through the live loops.
Because the simulation is consistent, the per-bin matrix recovery `G = Y·X⁻¹` returns the
open-loop coupled plant even though the data were taken closed — the controller is cancelled,
not fit. The diagonal FRF lands on the analytic oracle to a part in a thousand:

```{python}
#| label: fig-srm-diag
#| fig-cap: "Recovered diagonal element L→L of the open-loop plant, measured through the production damping loops: the rank-1 joint fit against the non-parametric estimate and the analytic oracle."
#| code-summary: "Recovered diagonal FRF (L→L) — fit vs nonparametric vs analytic oracle"
srm.diag_recovery_fig("L")
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Median diagonal recovery error vs the oracle"
display(Markdown(
    f"Median diagonal open-loop FRF error vs the analytic state-space oracle: "
    f"**{h.diag_rel:.4f}** (controller cancelled through the real L1-SRM loops)."))
```

The nonparametric `Y·X⁻¹` (grey markers) scatters near the resonances where the drive monitors
are small; the rank-1 joint fit (gold) passes through, sitting on the oracle (blue
dashed) through every mode and anti-resonance.

## The rank-1 joint MIMO modal fit

The parametric model shares one set of modal poles `(aₖ, bₖ)` across all 6×6 elements and gives
each mode a rank-1 residue `Rₖ = φₖ ψₖᵀ`. The fit is the package's sample-ML estimator with a
per-bin weighting, and its Cramér–Rao bound propagates to a per-mode `(f₀, Q)` uncertainty.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Recovered shared modal table — f0/Q ± CRB vs oracle"
display(srm.modal_table())
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-srm-modes
#| fig-cap: "Per-mode modal frequency residual (fit − oracle) with the Cramér–Rao σ."
#| code-summary: "Modal frequency recovery — fit − oracle with the CRB"
srm.modal_recovery_fig()
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Headline numbers"
display(Markdown(
    f"**{h.n_modes}** shared modal poles recovered at `df = {h.used_df:.4f} Hz`; median |Δf₀| vs "
    f"the oracle = **{h.df_med:.2f}%**, with a trustworthy CRB (dof = {h.dof} ≥ 14). "
    f"**{h.n_good} of {h.n_modes}** modes recover well in BOTH f₀ (|Δf|<1%) and Q (ΔQ<25%); "
    f"median Q-error = **{h.q_med:.1f}%** across the {h.n_wellsep} well-separated modes. "
    f"The well-separated modes (e.g. 0.848 Hz → Q=50.5, 2.038 Hz → Q=50.2) pin f₀ to <0.4% and Q "
    f"within a few % of the oracle's ~50."))
```

## What this shows — a resolved doublet and a calibrated CRB

Through the real production L1-SRM damping loops on the compiled twin, the open-loop coupled
plant comes back to 0.11% median diagonal error, and the joint fit returns 13 shared modal poles
with most Qs recovered to a few percent against a CRB. Two features warrant a careful reading
under the feasibility gate: the first is a resolved doublet, the second a calibrated bound.

### 1 · The tight 0.67 Hz "doublet" is spatial — and it resolves

The HSTS has a 0.672/0.676 Hz fundamental pair (~3 mHz, 0.5% apart). Under the shared-pole 6×6
model this pair collapses to a single pole — one pole set is forced across both modes, so the
fit returns one blended, biased fundamental (flagged in the table above). It is tempting to call
this a resolution limit. It is not. The HSTS plant block-diagonalizes exactly into two
orthogonal DOF planes — {L,P,V} and {T,R,Y} — with cross-plane FRF coupling ~1e-13 (machine
zero). The 0.6725 Hz mode lives purely in {L,P,V}; the 0.6758 Hz mode purely in {T,R,Y}. They are
near-coincident in frequency but separated by which sensors see them: a spatial doublet,
not a frequency split.

So we fit each plane alone. `mimo_fit.fit_block_decoupled` runs one rank-1 modal fit per plane;
each plane contains only one fundamental near 0.674 Hz, so there is no pair to collapse — and both
members come back on the oracle with a tight CRB, using no finer `df` and no
doublet-concentrated drive:

```{python}
#| label: fig-srm-doublet
#| fig-cap: "The 0.672/0.676 Hz pair in the (f₀, Q) plane. Under the shared-pole 6×6 model the pair collapses to one pole; the plane-decoupled fit separates it."
#| code-summary: "Shared-pole collapse vs the plane-decoupled fit, in the (f₀, Q) plane"
srm.doublet_resolved_fig()
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "The 0.67 Hz fundamental — collapsed vs plane-resolved vs oracle"
display(srm.doublet_table())
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "The numbers"
b = srm.doublet()
pa, pb, c = b.planes["{L,P,V}"], b.planes["{T,R,Y}"], b.collapsed
display(Markdown(
    f"The shared-pole fit blends the pair into a single **{c.f0:.4f} Hz** pole (Q {c.Q:.1f}), "
    f"off the oracle in both f₀ and Q. Fitting the two planes independently recovers **both** "
    f"members with no change to `df`: {{L,P,V}} at **{pa.f0:.4f} Hz** (Q {pa.Q:.1f}) and "
    f"{{T,R,Y}} at **{pb.f0:.4f} Hz** (Q {pb.Q:.1f}) — each within a few % of the oracle's "
    f"Q≈50, split by only Δf₀ ≈ {b.df_hz * 1e3:.1f} mHz."))
```

The collapse was a parameterization artifact of sharing one pole set across two orthogonal
modes — precisely the failure mode `CLAUDE.md`'s feasibility gate names — not a property of the
data. This exact resolution also runs portably, without the compiled twin — on the committed
reduced HSTS model (`system_ident/models/hsts_reduced_50hz.npz`, numpy-only): the same
`fit_block_decoupled` splits the 0.672/0.676 pair across the same two planes, guarded by
`tests/test_reduced_hsts_oracle.py`. (The one genuinely within-plane near-degeneracy — 1.512 & 1.527 Hz, both in {T,R,Y} — is
not resolved by the plane split; parametric ML super-resolves it given `SNR·N ≳ (Γ/Δf)⁴`, a finite
record-length/SNR cost, or a per-plane two-mode fit — see
[*Resolvability of two modes*](../tutorial/fisher.qmd#when-are-two-modes-resolvable), which
computes that cost from the CRB. That, too, is a cost to pay, not a wall.)

### 2 · The CRB is a process-disturbance bound

The compiled 6-DoF model exposes only
`DRIVE_EXC_<dof>` injection ports — there is no per-sensor readout-noise port like the
single-DoF `x1hsts`. A noise-free twin gives identical periods, so the P&S sample covariance
collapses to the floating-point floor and the bound is meaningless. To define a real CRB a small
broadband ground/actuator disturbance is injected on the non-driven drive ports; it propagates
through the real plant and dampers, making the spectra genuinely stochastic. The bound is
therefore self-consistent for the injected statistics — a process-disturbance CRB, not a
physical sensor-noise floor. The disturbance is small enough that the diagonal FRF still recovers
to 0.11%.
